title: How a cleaning business plan is structured
audience: Solo operators and owners writing or reviewing a business plan for a cleaning business in any Australian state or territory.
learningOutcomes: Name the sections a cleaning business plan needs, in order
Explain which decision each section supports
Label every number in a plan as a fact, a target or an assumption

instruction.heading: What the plan is for
instruction.body: A business plan is a working tool. It sets out what you will sell, who will buy it, how you will deliver it, what it will cost, and how you will know whether it is working. A bank, a landlord, a supplier or a large client may ask to see one, but the first reader should be you. If a section does not change a decision you will make, it does not need to be long.

instruction.heading: The sections and their jobs
instruction.body: A cleaning plan usually has ten parts. The executive summary is one page: what the business does, who it serves, where it works, who runs it and the headline goal. The mission states the standard you promise. The market section covers customer needs, competitors and trends. The marketing approach says how customers will find you. Objectives set marketing and financial targets with dates. The marketing mix covers pricing, service area, advertising and complaint handling. Positioning explains why a customer should choose you. Strategy sets the order of actions. Forecasts show break-even and sales by stage. Controls name what you measure, how often, and who checks it. Write the executive summary last, but place it first.

instruction.heading: How the sections depend on each other
instruction.body: The sections form a chain. The services you list decide the work, the work decides the hours, the hours decide the price, and the price together with your costs decides break-even. The staffing plan must match the forecast. If you change one link, check the others. A plan that promises a premium service but prices at the lowest rate in the market does not hang together, and a reader will notice before you do.

instruction.heading: Reading numbers honestly
instruction.body: Every number in a plan is one of three things. A fact is verified, such as an invoice or a signed contract. A target is what you want to reach, and it needs a date and a reason. An assumption is a belief you use for planning, and it needs a note on how you will test it. The sample plan this lesson draws on includes targets for growth, customer acquisition cost and overhead reduction with no workings shown. Treat those as targets and not as benchmarks. The sample is undated and written for a non-Australian market, so its figures are historical and are not current Australian data.

instruction.heading: Services: list only what you can deliver
instruction.body: Plans often list every service the owner has heard of. The sample plan includes laundering, ironing, and fumigation with pest control. Check the state and territory rules that apply to pest control and fumigation before any pesticide use. Before any regulated service appears in your plan, confirm the licence or authority needed in your state or territory, and whether you hold it. This lesson does not grant or describe any authority to carry out those services. Services you have not been trained or authorised to deliver should be marked as out of scope for now.

instruction.heading: Starting from a home
instruction.body: The sample plan proposes a home-based start for the first six months. Before you run any business from a residence, check what your local council allows, what your home and vehicle insurance covers, and what your lease or strata rules say.

procedure: Write the one-page executive summary last, then place it at the front of the document.
List the ten sections and write beside each one the decision it supports.
Draft each section in plain sentences, using local facts you have checked.
Tag every number as a fact, a target or an assumption, with a date and a source.
Check every listed service against the licence, training and insurance you hold, and mark any gap as out of scope.
Confirm the home-business, registration, tax and insurance points with the relevant authority, and leave them out until checked.
Set a review date three months ahead and record it in the plan.

workedExamples.situation: A sole cleaner in a regional town copies a sample plan that lists commercial cleaning, carpet cleaning and pest control. The owner has completed some training in cleaning methods and owns a vehicle, but has no pest control training.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which services go into the plan as offered now, and which go in as out of scope?
workedExamples.reasoning: Commercial and carpet cleaning are offered only if the owner has the training, equipment and insurance for them. Pest control is marked out of scope because the owner has no authority to deliver it, and the plan does not promise it to clients. The owner adds an open item to check the licence requirements before any future change.

equipmentAndPpe: Draft plan document with a version date
Register of licences, registrations and insurance held, with expiry dates

commonErrors.error: Copying a sample plan and keeping its figures
commonErrors.prevention: Replace each sample figure with one you have checked, or keep it as a labelled target with a reason.

commonErrors.error: Listing services the owner cannot lawfully or safely deliver
commonErrors.prevention: Check each service against licence, training and insurance before it appears in the offer.

commonErrors.error: Writing a long plan that nobody uses
commonErrors.prevention: Link each section to one decision, and remove any section that does not inform a decision.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Fumigation and pest control appear in the sample plan. In Australia these services are generally subject to state and territory licensing and pesticide rules. This lesson does not grant, describe or replace any licence or authority to perform these services.
Work health and safety duties apply to a business from its first job. Model WHS laws have been adopted in each state and territory, with local differences.
Check with the relevant Australian authority or a qualified adviser before relying on them.

qualityStandard: The plan contains all ten sections, in order, each with a named decision.
Every number is tagged as a fact, a target or an assumption, with a date and source.
No service is listed as offered unless the owner holds the licence, training and insurance it needs.
Every item still to be checked appears in one open-items table with an owner and a due date.
documentationEvidence: Plan document with version date and review date
Open-items table listing each point still to be checked
Licence, registration and insurance register with expiry dates
summary: A business plan is a set of linked decisions, not a template to fill in.
A service goes in the plan only once the owner can deliver it lawfully and safely.
Every number is labelled as a fact, a target or an assumption.
Sample figures are historical and non-Australian, and must not be used as current benchmarks.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which section should be written last but placed first in a cleaning business plan?
A sample plan lists pest control as a service. What is the correct action before the service appears in your offer?
options: Add it to the offer and set the price later and say it is licensed and fully insured
Subcontract the work and check the licence afterwards and add it to the offer now
Confirm the licence and authority required in your state or territory, and whether you hold it
Remove every licence reference from the plan and do not mention the work to clients

knowledgeChecks.question: A plan states that revenue will grow by a fixed percentage each year. How should the owner label that figure?
options: A fact, because it is written in the plan and it is in the sample
A target or assumption, with the reason and a review date recorded
A market statistic, because growth is common in the industry
Taxable income for the year and the tax due on it each year
